group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old man was evaluated late this morning in the ambulatory anesthesia clinic four days before a planned elective laparoscopic left inguinal hernia repair with mesh; the general surgeon anticipates a 60- to 75-minute procedure performed under general anesthesia with same-day discharge barring unexpected findings. The patient walked unassisted from the parking garage to the office, a distance he estimated at “two city blocks,” while carrying a briefcase and speaking in full sentences; he reports that on most evenings he completes a 3-mile leisurely neighborhood circuit at a pace that allows conversational breathing, mows his own lawn with a push mower, and climbs the single flight to his bedroom without needing to pause. He has never experienced substernal pressure, jaw or arm discomfort, exertional tightness, unexplained diaphoresis, or early fatigue that prompted cardiology evaluation, and he has not undergone stress imaging, coronary angiography, or intervention. He denies transient visual loss, focal weakness, slurred speech, or carotid procedures. His past medical history is dominated by type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 15 years ago after routine laboratory screening; initial dietary measures and metformin sufficed for approximately six years, but progressive fasting hyperglycemia led to the addition of NPH insulin at bedtime, subsequently transitioned to insulin glargine 28 units nightly with pre-meal insulin aspart doses calculated on a 1:12 carbohydrate ratio. Endocrinology follow-up one month ago documented a hemoglobin A1c of 7.2 %, and continuous glucose monitor downloads demonstrated 70 % time-in-range with rare nocturnal hypoglycemia promptly treated with juice. Additional conditions include well-controlled primary hypertension treated with lisinopril 20 mg each morning and amlodipine 5 mg nightly, mixed dyslipidemia on atorvastatin 40 mg daily, chronic allergic rhinitis managed with intranasal fluticasone, and gastroesophageal reflux disease relieved by omeprazole 20 mg. He underwent an uncomplicated appendectomy at age 25 and a screening colonoscopy five years ago that revealed two diminutive tubular adenomas removed endoscopically; no other surgeries are on record. There is no history of chronic kidney disease, although serum creatinine has slowly drifted upward over the last three years; the most recent nephrology note characterized the trend as consistent with mild diabetic nephropathy and emphasized blood pressure control. He quit cigarette smoking at age 35 after a 10-pack-year exposure, drinks one bottle of beer with dinner on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. A first-degree relative experienced a myocardial infarction at 71, and his mother died of breast cancer at 78. Review of systems today is negative for palpitations, presyncope, ankle swelling, claudication, fevers, night sweats, weight loss, or gastrointestinal bleeding. After five minutes seated, vital signs are oral temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg in the right arm, radial pulse 72 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air; body mass index calculated from height 178 cm and weight 88 kg is 27.8 kg/m². He appears comfortable, converses easily, and has no accessory muscle use. Neck examination reveals supple cervical range of motion and no carotid bruits; jugular venous contour is not assessed in detail because he is seated upright. The precordial impulse is nondisplaced, and auscultation identifies a crisp first and second heart sound without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear to vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. Abdomen is soft with a palpable, easily reducible 3-cm left inguinal bulge that enlarges on cough impulse but shows no tenderness, skin changes, or incarceration. Extremities are warm with 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and no edema or calf tenderness. Neurologic screening demonstrates intact cranial nerves, symmetrical strength, brisk deep tendon reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and pinprick, and a steady tandem gait. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour prior to the visit reveal hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, platelet count 232 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.3 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.32 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 61 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting plasma glucose obtained in the same sample is 128 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 25 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, and international normalized ratio 1.0. A 12-lead electrocardiogram performed in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats per minute, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, QTc 410 ms, and no Q waves, ST-segment deviations, or T-wave inversions. Upright posterior-anterior chest radiograph reveals clear lung fields, normal cardiomediastinal silhouette, and no diaphragmatic elevation or free air. Airway assessment by anesthesia records a Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor distance of 4.5 cm, and full atlanto-occipital extension; no loose teeth are noted. The patient has been instructed to continue lisinopril, amlodipine, atorvastatin, and basal insulin as scheduled, to administer 50 % of the usual glargine dose the evening before surgery, omit pre-meal insulin on the morning of the operation unless point-of-care glucose exceeds 200 mg/dL, to stop solid food eight hours before induction while allowing clear liquids until two hours pre-arrival, and to bring his glucometer and sensor receiver on the day of surgery for peri-operative glucose management. After an extensive discussion covering potential risks of anesthesia, bleeding, wound infection, postoperative urinary retention, and glycemic excursions, the patient voiced understanding, asked pertinent questions regarding return to exercise, and expressed readiness to proceed with the scheduled repair.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular): the planned inguinal hernia repair is not classified as high risk here → 0.
- Ischemic heart disease: no known coronary disease, angina, or pathologic Q waves → 0.
- Heart failure: no history or clinical evidence → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA reported → 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: uses glargine and aspart → 1.
- Creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: measured 1.32 mg/dL → 0.
Total = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 1.
Final answer: 1
